geo.title: The end-Cretaceous impact and the beginning of the Cenozoic
geo.ageBasis: Global K–Pg boundary; ages follow the ICS 2026/06 timescale.
geo.fact: Impact ejecta in the global boundary layer coincide with the extinction horizon, supporting the Chicxulub impact as the trigger of the mass extinction. Cenozoic ecological reconstruction began with lineages that survived the crisis; 66 Ma is a chronostratigraphic boundary, and ecological recovery was not completed simultaneously in every region.
geo.limitation: The timing of the disappearance and recovery of individual groups is affected by depositional gaps and sampling resolution.

history.title: Sealings and storage management at Sabi Abyad

sources.author: Peter M.M.G. Akkermans and Kim Duistermaat

geo.title: Early stem primates appear in post-extinction forests
geo.ageBasis: C29r in Montana, USA; the study constrains the record to 105–139 ka after the K–Pg boundary.
geo.fact: Teeth from Montana place the reliable record of Purgatorius very shortly after the extinction, showing that arboreal omnivorous to fruit-eating niches were already becoming established. This record provides a minimum age constraint on the early radiation of the primate total group; its actual origin could still predate the known fossil record.
geo.limitation: The evidence consists mainly of teeth; phylogenetic placement and an inferred Cretaceous origin still require additional evidence.

geo.title: Terrestrial communities in Colorado recover gradually
geo.ageBasis: Dated Corral Bluffs section: approximately 0.1–0.7 Ma after the boundary.
geo.fact: In a continuous section, mammalian diversity and maximum body size increased gradually after the extinction, with larger members appearing within about 700,000 years alongside a record of legumes. geo.limitation: A section from one region cannot represent the global pace of recovery; the first appearance of plants is also affected by preservation.

geo.title: Robust early placentals occupy ground-dwelling niches
geo.ageBasis: Torrejonian fossils from New Mexico; the broad interval encloses the ages of the occurrences.
geo.fact: Periptychus had robust limbs, a plantigrade stance, and strongly ornamented teeth, showing the expansion of functional morphology in early placentals. geo.limitation: Climbing and digging abilities are inferred from morphology; different functions can share the same skeletal features.
